analytic.title: Towards Early Performance Assessment Based on UML MARTE Models for Distributed Systems

div.p: Distributed systems are the current solution for large and complex systems. Their main disadvantage is the communication delay which has to be controlled, otherwise they may become unusable. Early performance assessment, by using tools which process system models, helps in making informed design decisions. The new standard in time-critical systems is MARTE (Modeling and Analysis of Real-Time and Embedded systems), adopted in 2008 by OMG (Object Management Group) as a new UML (Unified Modeling Language) profile [11]. This paper focuses on automatic extraction of performance models from UML models, with MARTE annotations; most of the existing analysis tools are still based on the now obsolete SPT (Schedulability, Performance and Time) profile. The envisioned tool should be versatile and accept several types of diagrams, since UML allows a multitude of system views. The output performance model should be easy to refine either into an analytical model or into a simulation one. However, only the relevant information from the UML model should be stored in the performance model, in order to improve analysis efficiency. The outcome of this research activity is building a tool that combines flexibility and conciseness, while being suitable for performance analysis.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Computer networks in general and the Internet in particular provide the means to build advanced systems, extensible both horizontally (large range of offered services) and vertically (complex and intensive processing). Distributed systems make this possible by using resources, such as storage and computing power, from several interconnected host computers. However, drawbacks exist too, one coming exactly from the need to share resources: clear access policies need to be enforced and complex resource management leads to higher latency in processing nodes. A more important problem is the communication delay which cannot be avoided. This aspect presents a high risk because the current trend in object-oriented technologies is to make object location transparent. Thus, remote messages can be considered equivalent to local messages and communication delay is ignored. This is a common mistake during system design, and it may lead to unforeseen performance problems. Effects of such delays are noticed only after deployment, when the system becomes unusable, especially in high load conditions that occur in real network traffic. This kind of behavior can be predicted by analysis, in high traffic conditions, of system models, which include object location information.

Early performance assessment, based on system models, helps make informed design decisions; delay issues are detected when the efforts for fixing them are still reasonable. The cost of design changes increases as the project evolves towards deployment; usually, a change in design is unfeasible after the system has been deployed.
Performance evaluation assumes obtaining performance parameters, such as response time, throughput and resource utilization, based on preliminary information about the system.

Automation of the process, by using performance evaluation tools, speeds-up the analysis and also compensates for the expertise that developers need not have in the field of performance analysis. Tools have specific input and output models, described in a standard format; Unified Modeling Language (UML) has been chosen, since it is a widely adopted modeling language.

AADL (Architecture Analysis Description Language) was adopted in 2004 for time-critical systems definition and analysis, but it requires a detailed system design. In 2008, MARTE (Modeling and Analysis of Real-Time and Embedded systems) was adopted by OMG as a new UML profile. It is preferred because it does not require too many design details, so the analysis can be performed at a higher level, and thus earlier in the project lifecycle. [12] This paper focuses on automatic extraction of performance models from UML models, with MARTE annotations. Most of the existing analysis tools are based on the now obsolete SPT (Schedulability, Performance and Time) profile [10], the predecessor of MARTE.

A new analysis tool is to be developed, based on the UML extensions from the MARTE profile. The tool should be versatile by interpreting the meaning of several types of diagrams; UML allows a multitude of system views, meaning that a system may be defined in several different ways.

In order to build a MARTE-compliant performance analysis tool, the input files will need to be provided by a design tool, with visual diagram editing features. The design tool will save the model in XMI format, and the analysis tool will parse such XMI files as input.
Concerning the extracted performance model, there are two types of such models: analytical and simulation models.

Analytical models are mathematical representations of the system, which are solved in order to obtain performance results. Simulation models are executable systems that behave similar to the system Figure 1. Classes in the Core Scenario Model meta-model [8] being developed and performance results are measured by running these models.

The analysis tool will extract a performance model that should be easy to refine either into an analytical model or into a simulation one. A very good starting point is CSM (Core Scenario Model) [8]. Only the relevant information from the UML model should be stored in the performance model, in order to improve analysis efficiency; items which do not have any performance annotations will be ignored.
The outcome of this research activity is building a tool that combines flexibility and conciseness, while being suitable for performance analysis.

In section II, the main research approaches regarding performance models, both analytical and simulation approaches are addressed, and a few UML 2 based performance analysis applications are described. The MARTE UML profile is briefly presented in section III, along with a few applications that are able to provide a visual design interface, in order to draw UML 2 diagrams, possibly with MARTE annotations. The transformation of these diagrams into a new, concise and flexible, performance model is explained in section IV. Finally, section V shows conclusions and directions of future research.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: The domain of SPE (Software Performance Engineering) has been studied over the last two decades: the first methodologies were defined at a slower pace during the '90s, while the important tools have had a rather fast evolution after year 2000.

div.head: A. Performance Models
div.p: Among the analytical approaches, the most frequently implemented in tools (model solvers) are the following: Execution Graphs (EG), Markov chains generated from system definitions using ADL (Architectural Description Language), Stochastic Timed Petri Nets (STPN), Queueing Networks (QN), and their extensions called Extended Queueing Networks (EQN) and Layered Queueing Networks (LQN).

Since several different performance models can be derived from the same set of specifications, the idea of having a common representation occurred. Then, this common intermediate representation could be transformed into any kind of analytical model.

An important intermediate model is the Core Scenario Model (CSM) [8], which extracts relevant performance information stored implicitly and explicitly in UML diagrams and SPT profile data [10]. The desired performance model is obtained by two transformations: UML model to CSM (U2C) and CSM to Performance model (C2P). Query/View/Transformation (QVT) of Meta Object Facility (MOF) is recommended to define these transformations, but, due to lack of tools to support this language, XSLT (Extensible Stylesheet Transformations) was used, operating on models represented in XML format.

The CSM meta-model provides explicit representation for entities that are required in order to build performance models, as shown in Fig. 1; it is consistent with MOF. The first phase, U2C, consists of converting Deployment and Activity diagrams into CSM: input consists of XMI files representing the UML model; the CSM internal representation is a DOM (Domain Object Model) tree that can be exported in XML format.

Regarding the second phase -transformation of CSM to a performance model -a systematic algorithm to convert a scenario model UCM (Use Case Map) -almost identical to CSM -into a LQN model is described in [7]. This algorithm has been implemented in the UCM2LQN tool.

Another approach in transforming annotated UML models into LQN models uses an intermediate model (IM) represented as an XML tree [3]. This model was developed in parallel with CSM, so it has similar features, but unlike CSM, it is a task-based model -steps are grouped into tasks, rather than into scenarios.

An example of IM is shown in Fig. 2. The input, expressed as UML (in XMI format), is converted into IM based on an algorithm that maps UML nodes and states (from Activity diagrams) to IM concepts (some of these are shown in Fig. 2). Figure 3. The UML-Ψ model processing framework [5] Figure 4. The UML-Ψ model processing framework [5] Simulation-based performance analysis tools rely on an internal simulation model, built from the system specifications (entered either in a visual manner, by drawing diagrams, or in XMI format). An important tool developed by Marzolla as the application part of his PhD thesis [5] is UML-PSI (UML Performance SImulator), described in detail in [6]. UML Performance Simulator is a tool that builds a simulation model and runs it in order to collect performance information. The overall structure of the tool is presented in Fig. 3.

Tool input consists in XMI files exported by ArgoUML (or the commercial version Poseidon), a visual tool for defining UML diagrams. The diagrams are annotated with performance information according to the UML SPT profile [10]. UML-Ψ extracts relevant information from the XMI input file and generates a performance processoriented simulation model, based on three main types of entities, corresponding to scenario actions (from Activity diagrams), the resources of the software system (from Deployment diagrams) and the workloads (from Use Case diagrams).

The simulation model execution can be customized from a configuration file, written in Perl, which usually defines simulation parameters, such as simulation duration and desired accuracy of results, and also provides values for unbounded variables in the UML model.

Performance results are inserted into the software model as tagged values for relevant UML elements. The feedback mechanism is immediate since there is a clear correspondence between the software model and the simulation model, as shown in Fig. 4. The mapping is somewhat similar to CSM.
After having reviewed the most relevant approaches regarding performance models, in the following paragraphs the latest tools based on UML 2 or MARTE will be presented.

div.head: B. UML 2 or MARTE Compliant Tools
div.p: Recently, a MARTE compliant performance evaluation tool was developed as a plug-in for Rational Software Architect (RSA) v7, based on the implementation of the MARTE profile for RSA, available at the OMG MARTE web site [13]. The tool, described in [9], implements an algorithm that converts the user-provided UML MARTE model into a Performance Evaluation Process Algebra (PEPA) model, which can further be evaluated by solving the underlying Continuous Time Markov Chain (CTMC).

A simulation tool that uses UML 2 diagrams is DESMO-J (Discrete-Event Simulation and Modeling in Java). N. Knaak and B. Page explain the benefits of using UML 2 in [4] and express their intention to adopt them as input for DESMO-J. Diagram types and their utility are briefly described (structural, behavior, and interaction diagrams) and Activity Diagrams are then presented in more detail. They are said to be useful in DES, providing means for both event-based simulation -modeling event routines -and process-based simulation -modeling the lifecycle of simulation processes, using features such as concurrency, object flow and message passing.

V. Cortellessa has implemented MOSES (Modeling Software and platform architEcture in UML 2 for Simulation-based performance analysis), a methodology that accomplishes integration of software models with platform models, in order to devise meaningful performance models [2]. This approach allows estimating the performance of the same software architecture on multiple platform architectures without underlying (possibly incorrect) model transformations. Instead of such transformations, this methodology integrates in one notation software and platform models plus annotations, thus building a performance model in the same notation. Tool support was needed for visual modeling and simulation: Telelogic Tau G2 was chosen because it also provides a language -SDL (Standard and Description Language) to describe Statecharts and to model actions. Hence, specification of platform details (needed for performance analysis) can be delayed -SDL blocks can be inserted at a later time, not necessarily at software design time.

Since UML 2 and MARTE were recently adopted, there are few analysis tools relying on them. This is the reason for which an approach needs to be defined concerning the [11] way MARTE notations can be mapped to a flexible, generic performance model, a synthesis of the intermediate models presented at the beginning of this section.

div.head: III. THE MARTE PROFILE
div.p: The main packages and notions that are relevant for performance analysis will be presented and then a few tools with visual design facilities are reviewed.

div.head: A. Profile Description
div.p: MARTE is a replacement for the SPT profile. The latter provides a grammar for powerful concepts (symbolic variables and time expressions), but does not support userdefined NFPs and specialized domains. The MARTE NFP (NonFunctional Properties) modeling framework reuses structural concepts in QoS&FT (Quality of Service & Fault Tolerance), but reduces the usage complexity; also, it introduces VSL (Value Specification Language) which extends and formalizes concepts from TVL (Tag Value Language, defined in SPT).
Besides the NFP, Time and Core Elements, there is a package which provides notions to define the execution platform: Generic Resource Modeling (GRM).

The basis for all analysis packages is the Generic Quantitative Analysis Modeling (GQAM) package that defines basic modeling concepts and NFPs. Many stereotypes defined in this package are useful for performance analysis.

The Performance Analysis Profile (PAM) comes with a few specific stereotypes and tagged values. This package provides means to express the input and output of performance analysis methodologies. As input, UML diagrams are used, with well-defined extensions for performance related annotations (parameters, such as request arrival rate, mean execution time for external operations). These are called parameterized NFPs and are used to define variations that may occur in the studied system, defined in a certain AnalysisContext. The AnalysisContext consists of system behavior (scenarios), resources and workload. Also, platform specific (environment) information should be provided as input in order to allow for certain analysis methods (like simulation) to be carried on accurately. There are predefined libraries with models for middleware or operating systems and they can be integrated into the system model. Output can also be expressed as NFPs of the UML model elements: response time of scenarios, utilization of resources, throughput (especially for communication resources, expressed in operations/second). The main extensions in the package are illustrated in Fig. 5, along with the basic types defined in GQAM.

div.head: B. Implementation in Visual Design Tools
div.p: There several design tools that are UML 2 compliant: Poseidon for UML (Gentleware), TAU G2 (Telelogic), Visual Paradigm for UML, Rational Software Modeler (IBM), Together (Borland).

Since the adoption of the MARTE profile, only one open-source design tool was developed, that supports it: Papyrus UML [14], and this is the tool that will provide input XMI files for the analysis tool, at least for the moment, until a better design tool is implemented.

The tool allows for MARTE stereotypes to be applied to UML elements and also provides a graphical interface for declaration of tagged values. The only drawback is that not all basic UML 2 properties can be modified (for example, "joinSpec" for a Join node in Activity diagrams). Another visual editing feature that would be helpful concerns data types, such as ArrivalPattern, specified in MARTE as strings (VSL). It would be easier for the user to edit them as composite types, by accessing each component and providing the value. However, this is not in the scope of the current paper, so the focus will remain on building the performance model.

div.head: IV. PERFORMANCE MODEL DEFINITION AND
div.p: EXTRACTION The first step in building the performance analysis tool was the study of an existing one, UML-Ψ, and the proof of the utility for performance analysis [1]. The simulation model it implements is simple enough to be easily extracted from the input UML model with SPT annotations.

One of the intentions of this paper is to find a flexible and simple model, that can easily be adapted to suit both analytical and simulation approaches. Firstly, reference models from both approaches were chosen: the simulation model from UML-Ψ and an analytical intermediate model (since such a model can further be transformed into several other analytical models, as shown in the Related Work section) -CSM. Fortunately, the two selected models are somewhat similar, so the new performance model is derived in a straightforward manner and is shown in Fig. 6.
The next step is to establish how this model can be extracted from UML diagrams, with MARTE annotations.

From the multitude of ways to define a system, only specific combinations are considered to provide a meaningful system representation for performance analysis. In the following paragraphs, for each of these sets of diagrams, the process of extracting the performance model will be described.

The resources, both active and passive, are specified by Deployment Diagrams; the performance related elements should be stereotyped as GaExecHost (GQAM), SchedulableResource (GRM), or just Resource (GRM)for passive resources. An example of a deployment diagram is presented in Fig. 7.

The performance model will include two objects of type ActiveResource: Service1 and App1 (these are software applications); they run on specific platforms (GaExecHost), which may be considered resources themselves, but they will only be used by the previously mentioned active resources (as their host property); this is a two-layer deployment.
In order to maintain compatibility with models defined in SPT, the tool will also accept simplified Deployment Diagrams, such as the one in Fig. 8.
In this case, each object stereotyped as GaExecHost will become an ActiveResource, and each object stereotyped as Resource will become a PassiveResource.

In order to add behavior to these resources, there are In case of single-layered deployment, the "host" property indicates the GaExecHost resource, and for doublelayered deployment the "concurRes" property refers to a SchedulableResource.

A Sequence Diagram is a scenario itself, because it provides successive calls (steps) among instances of resources. Each message stereotyped as PaStep is a step that executes on the resource given by the lifeline towards which it is headed. This lifeline belongs to an item stereotyped as PaRunTInstance, having a tagged value called "instance" that points to a SchedulableResource (in case of double-layered deployment), and also a "host" property that specifies a GaExecHost (for single-layered deployment). The workload is usually defined by the first message in the sequence, stereotyped as WorkloadEvent.

The complete performance model is obtained by applying the above mentioned mapping rules to diagrams and to the properly stereotyped items and their specific tagged values. The guidelines are summarized in Table I, omitting tagged values mapping rules, covered previously.

div.head: V. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: The SPE domain has been subject to continuous evolution because of the increasing awareness regarding the importance performance has for present software systems, especially during system development. At the rate at which systems become obsolete nowadays, there is no time to fix performance related issues once the system has been deployed.

Performance analysis requires time and expertise, resources that software developers do not have, so automation via tools is very useful in this domain. These tools can embed the performance modeling and analysis knowledge, which is not familiar to most developers; also, automation of this evaluation process saves precious time. This paper sets the basis for implementing such a performance analysis tool, which accepts as input XMI files generated by a visual diagram editor -Papyrus UML [14]. A new performance model is derived from two representative models, one for the analytical approach, CSM [8], and one for the simulation approach, UML-Ψ [6]. This model is concise, by eliminating redundant elements, and also flexible, because it resembles both analytical and simulation models.

The next step in the tool development is using this intermediate model to define a more efficient, hybrid model. This will lead to more accurate and faster performance analysis, by comparison to pure analytical or simulation approaches.

figure.figDesc: Scenario flows are described as ordered sequences of steps and PathConnection objects which connect each pair of steps. Sequence objects connect consecutive steps, Branch and Merge objects define alternative steps (ORfork, OR-join), while for parallel activities (AND-fork, AND-join) there are Fork and Join objects. Each PathConnection object has m source steps and n target steps, n and m depend on the particular object subtype. Messages could have been used related to network communication, but they were not supported in UML SPT. Each step is executed by an active resource, which may be a device (ProcessingResource) or an operation provided by an external subsystem (ExternalService).Steps can handle passive resources, including processes or threads in an operating system, hosted by ProcessingResources. Several step types can be distinguished, such as Start, End, ResourceAcquire and ResourceRelease; the first step of a scenario (Start) may be associated to a workload. This kind of subtyping improves model checking and performance model generation.

two possibilities: Use Case Diagram or Sequence Diagram. A Use Case Diagram connects actors to use cases (behavior). An actor stereotyped as WorkloadEvent will become a Workload (open or closed) in the performance model, while a use case (stereotyped as GaScenario) will become a Scenario (a composite step). The scenario can be defined either by an Activity Diagram, or a State Machine Diagram. Each Activity/State stereotyped with PaStep will become a Step, while each Control Flow/Transition will become a Transition in the performance model. Fork and Join nodes are treated as pseudo-actions. Branch and Merge nodes need not be considered as distinct steps, because multiple outgoing or incoming transitions may be defined for each step, and the probability, in case of Branch, is included in the Transition object. The ActiveResource for each step is extracted from the tagged values of the PaStep stereotype.
